title: Digital deception detection & COVID-19: Exploring Mediated Statement Analysis (MSA) application to truthful & untruthful pandemic-related social media posts
Digital Brand Communication in the African Economy: A Critical Review of Theory, Practice, and Emerging Issues
venue: British Journal of Mass Communication and Media Research
abstract: With digital technology significantly revolutionizing the way organizations interact with their customers, digital brand communication has become one of the most critical components that can help organizations develop a competitive edge and build long-term relationships with their customers. Even though digital communication has been rapidly developing in the modern world, there is little understanding of digital brand communication in Africa and specifically in Nigeria through the prism of the relevant academic literature. The purpose of this review paper is to analyse the development, theoretical background, drivers, and perspectives of digital brand communication in Africa. Using an approach of narrative integrative review, this paper critically examines existing literature available in various disciplines such as communication, marketing, branding, and information systems in order to gain insight into the concept of digital brand communication in the new digital ecosystem. Some of the key factors that determine effective digital brand communication are social media marketing, personal communication, content marketing, influencer marketing, user generated content, electronic word of mouth, artificial intelligence, omnichannel communication, and mobile first engagement. Digital brand communication is constrained by infrastructural constraints, digital inequality, privacy issues, cyber security threats, regulatory concerns, and cultural diversity. Through the synthesis of Relationship Marketing Theory, Consumer Engagement Theory, and the Technology Acceptance Model, a comprehensive theoretical framework for digital brand communication in Africa is proposed by this study. This literature review adds to the body of knowledge through its analysis of digital brand communication in relation to the African context, the development of a comprehensive perspective, and a research agenda that can be used in future research. The results of the study are valuable in their recommendations for the design of ethical and consumer-centric digital branding that could build brand equity and competitive advantage in Africa.

title: Toward safer digital sexual health communication: evaluating the public health reliability of large language model responses on sexually transmitted infections
abstract:
Background 
                     The global burden of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) continues to rise, yet stigma drives many to seek sensitive health information from artificial intelligence chatbots. The quality, safety, readability, and destigmatization of large language model (LLM) responses on sexual health remain under-evaluated, particularly for non-Western models. 
                   
                   
                     Methods 
                     This cross-sectional study constructed 30 standardized English queries (5 themes × 6 questions) informed by Google Trends, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) guidelines, and patient education platforms, and submitted them to three LLMs—GPT-5.4, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and Kimi K2.6—via official APIs, in duplicate (180 responses). Two dermatovenereologists (&gt;10 years' experience) rated the responses while blinded to platform identity, across six dimensions (accuracy, completeness, safety, understandability, actionability, and destigmatization) using a five-point scale, supplemented by four readability metrics (FKGL, FRE, GFI, and SMOG). Primary analysis used linear mixed-effects models retaining all individual ratings; the original aggregated non-parametric pipeline was retained as a sensitivity analysis. Reliability used ICC and quadratic-weighted Cohen's κ with 95% CIs; correlations used query-level cluster bootstrap with false-discovery-rate control. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     
                      Inter-platform differences were significant for accuracy (χ

                      = 0.041). GPT-5.4 and Kimi K2.6 achieved the highest accuracy (both median 5.00), both significantly above DeepSeek-V4-Pro and not significantly different from each other. DeepSeek-V4-Pro and Kimi K2.6 both used significantly more destigmatizing language than GPT-5.4, with no significant difference between them.                      Conclusions 
                     The three LLMs showed distinct profiles: GPT-5.4 and Kimi K2.6 achieved the highest accuracy, whereas GPT-5.4 produced the least readable outputs; DeepSeek-V4-Pro and Kimi K2.6 used more destigmatizing language. To our knowledge, this is the first study to quantify destigmatizing language as an explicit evaluation dimension for LLM-generated STI content, albeit as an exploratory measure pending formal content validation. Findings are specific to these models and queries and can inform quality standards and monitoring for safer AI-powered sexual health communication.

title: Framing Insecurity in North-West Nigeria: A Conceptual Analysis of Social Media Actors and Nigeria Police Force Narratives
venue: Azman University International Journal of Management and Social Sciences
abstract: The proliferation of social media has transformed the communication ecology of insecurity in North-West Nigeria by enabling citizens, journalists, security agencies, and non-state actors to compete in framing conflicts. While the Nigeria Police Force (NPF) seeks to frame insecurity through official narratives emphasizing operational successes, public reassurance, and institutional legitimacy, social media actors frequently construct alternative frames highlighting government failure, human suffering, insecurity, and distrust in state institutions. This conceptual paper examines the competing frames employed by social media actors and the Nigeria Police in communicating insecurity across Northern Nigeria. Guided by Framing Theory, the study adopts a conceptual research design based on documentary analysis of scholarly publications, government reports, media studies, and policy documents. The paper argues that framing contests between institutional and citizen-generated narratives significantly shape public perceptions of insecurity, confidence in security institutions, and national discourse on conflict management. The study concludes that while social media democratizes security communication by amplifying marginalized voices, it also accelerates misinformation, emotional polarization, and competing truth claims. Conversely, official police communication often prioritizes institutional legitimacy over transparency, thereby widening public distrust. The paper recommends adopting evidence-based strategic communication, collaborative digital engagement, and transparent crisis communication to enhance public confidence and strengthen democratic policing in Nigeria.

title: Empowerment or exploitation? reconsidering women's social media entrepreneurship in the gig economy
abstract: Social media has fundamentally transformed contemporary entrepreneurial practices. Social media platforms like Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, Pinterest and YouTube have allowed people to set up businesses that require minimal startup capital and a quick reach to people around the world. Social media has significantly influenced women's entrepreneurial participation in the economy, creative selfemployment and flexible working opportunities, with the propensity to increasingly engage in these activities through digital platforms (Ghosh et al., 2022).However, more recently, the creation of what is called the creator economy and platform mediated entrepreneurship has further shifted social media from a promotional tool to an entrepreneurial infrastructure that now impacts on the visibility of creators, their engagement with audiences, monetisation of their content, and how the entrepreneurs' commercial sustainability is shaped (B. E. Duffy & Meisner, 2023;van Dijck et al., 2018). Although these developments have brought new possibilities for women entrepreneurs to sell their products in markets and develop sustainable digital ventures, they have also exacerbated the reliance on market platforms and algorithmic visibility, as well as on ongoing communicative labour. Today, entrepreneurial success increasingly depends on entrepreneurs' ability to navigate platform rules, cultivate audience relationships, and adapt strategically to evolving platform ecosystems.Social media has significantly expanded entrepreneurial opportunities for women by lowering barriers to market entry, reducing start-up costs, and facilitating direct access to geographically dispersed consumers (Ghosh et al., 2022). These affordances have enabled women to establish creative enterprises, cultivate entrepreneurial identities, and participate more actively in digital economies. At the same time, entrepreneurial success increasingly depends not only on business capability but also on sustained platform visibility, audience engagement, and algorithmically mediated communication. Communication therefore becomes more than a promotional activity; it constitutes a productive form of entrepreneurial labour through which visibility, legitimacy, and commercial sustainability are continuously negotiated within platform ecosystems.The developments are a sign of the fact that social media entrepreneurship is more than a technology or an economic phenomenon. Instead, platform governance, communicative work, and algorithmic visibility are now more and more vital aspects of entrepreneurial achievement. Thus, a conceptual model is needed that is able to reflect both entrepreneurial opportunity and platform dependency in the entrepreneurial experience of women.The aim of the opinion paper is to rethink social media entrepreneurship of women, looking at it from the lens of platform capitalism, digital labour, feminist media studies and communication studies. Instead of entrepreneurship being merely a means for empowerment, this paper suggests that the success of the entrepreneur depends more and more on communicative labour, emotional branding and algorithmic visibility. Building upon recent discussions of platform-dependent entrepreneurship (Yu & Sekiguchi, 2024), this paper proposes the Platform-Dependent Woman Entrepreneur as a communication-centred conceptual framework that extends existing theory by foregrounding the gendered communicative, emotional, and algorithmically mediated dimensions of entrepreneurial dependence within platform economies.There are a few studies that have contributed to our knowledge of digital entrepreneurs, platform workers, influencers and content creators, but none has addressed the full range of these roles. However, as a social media entrepreneur, a woman holds a unique position in platform economies as she is not only a business owner but is also structurally dependent on privately-controlled digital platforms for demonstrating her entrepreneurial visibility, reaching audiences and achieving commercial viability. While working in platform business markets, women entrepreneurs have to negotiate algorithmic visibility, communicative expectations, and emotional performances as well as business management, in contrast to conventional entrepreneurs who are mainly impacted by their competitive capability. Feminist scholarship also indicates that women's experiences of platform participation are often distinct from men's due to the expectation that women are more authentic, emotional, responsive, aesthetic and vulnerable to online gendered hostility when visible as entrepreneurs. Hence, platform dependency should be seen not only as a dependency on technological aspects, but also as a dependency on gendered communicative expectations that give rise to opportunities and constraints for the entrepreneur. Entrepreneurship in social media is fundamentally different from traditional business entrepreneurial activity since entrepreneurial value is not just from the production and exchange of goods and services, it is generated from a continuous communicative interaction with platform ecosystems. Entrepreneurs should be aware of visibility, audience engagement, platform insights, and continuously evolve their communication approach for algorithmic-driven spaces. Thus, communicative, relational and affective activities become fundamental parts of entrepreneurial activity, instead of marketing. As such, from a digital labour perspective entrepreneurial communication is a productive labour which creates value for both the entrepreneur and the digital platforms (Gajjala, 2018;Terranova, 2000). Women's social media entrepreneurship, therefore, should not be considered only as an activity of participating in the market but also as a participation in the platforms-based labour system, whose success is increasingly based on the need for ongoing communicative performance.In digital economies, the distinction between productive labour, self-expression, identity performance and leisure have gotten increasingly blurred, as digital labour itself has long maintained (Terranova, 2000). Women entrepreneurs are a great example of this shift as entrepreneurial success is becoming more and more dependent on their ability to create content, engage in social media, tell a story, and build their own brand as an internet personality as well as a business owner. These communicative practices create economic value for both the entrepreneur and the platform owners, the audience and the advertisers, thus, perpetuating the quasidependence of the entrepreneur on the algorithms and systems of visibility that run through the platform (B. E. Duffy & Meisner, 2023;van Dijck et al., 2018).In addition to productive labour, women entrepreneurs engage in a lot of affective and relational labour by interacting with their audience, managing their community, being emotionally responsive to their audience and building trust with their audience. Feminist scholarship has long established that these kinds of labour are expected mainly of women since entrepreneurial success is often seen as being related to authenticity and emotional accessibility, not just entrepreneurial competence (Gill, 2007;Hochschild, 2012). While they are largely hidden in traditional entrepreneurship studies, these communication practices are essential for economic value because they help to keep audiences loyal, keep people on the platform and help to preserve entrepreneurial continuity.The feminisation of communicative labour is particularly evident in the realm of creator cultures, where technology has led to the development of para-social relationships, where women entrepreneurs must be constantly in touch with followers, must share a part of their life and must demonstrate emotional authenticity in becoming a successful entrepreneur. Such labour goes far beyond simply the promotion; it's an investment that creates the visibility, trust, engagement and value of platforms all at once. Communication then serves more than just as a facilitator of entrepreneurial activity, it is also economically productive labour that is engaged in the reproduction of entrepreneurial identities and commercial sustainability.Digital labour therefore provides an important explanation for how entrepreneurial value is produced within platform economies. However, understanding women's entrepreneurship requires moving beyond digital labour alone to examine how algorithmic governance, platform dependency, and communicative expectations jointly shape entrepreneurial opportunities and constraints.Today, being platform-dependent has become a major characteristic of social media entrepreneurship. Social media entrepreneurs rely on entrepreneurial visibility, audience reach, and commercial sustainability, unlike traditional businesses which compete mostly in terms of their products, services, or positioning in the market, and rely on private and self-governing digital infrastructures that regulate their visibility, audience, and sustainability. Platform algorithms not only influence entrepreneurship opportunities but also the entrepreneurial strategic capabilities of the entrepreneurs themselves, as they determine what is visible, discoverable and thus economically worthwhile in the platforms (Bucher, 2018;Gillespie, 2019).Entrepreneurial success is therefore increasingly tied to the ability of entrepreneurs to constantly adjust to the changing recommendations systems, platform policies and algorithmic governance.There is a basic paradox associated with platform dependency. Digital platforms significantly lower the cost of entry into entrepreneurship, as they offer low-cost access to markets and audiences, as well as to digital infrastructures. Meanwhile, they concentrate visibility, monetisation, and the access of audiences into their own closed and algorithm-driven systems, which they keep mostly hidden from entrepreneurs. For entrepreneurs, the outcome of their business can change drastically due to changes in their algorithmic recommendations, content moderation or even monetisation policies, without anything changing in their entrepreneurial ability or product quality (Cotter, 2019;B. E. Duffy & Meisner, 2023). But entrepreneurial risk is now more and more governed via platform control mechanisms as opposed to just market competition. Entrepreneurial sustainability is thus more than an enhancement of entrepreneurial competence, and relies on the ability to negotiate ongoing algorithmic uncertainty, as the entrepreneur's job.Although platform dependency explains entrepreneurs' structural reliance upon digital infrastructures, entrepreneurial success is ultimately realised through communication. Visibility, legitimacy, and commercial sustainability emerge through communicative practices that continually translate algorithmic exposure into audience relationships and economic value.In platform economies, the function of communication is not only to promote but to become a productive entrepreneurial practice as well. In addition to creating products or providing services, entrepreneurs have to constantly tell stories about themselves, new audiences, remain visible, and create a continuity of communication on platforms. Algorithmic visibility thus makes communication an economically productive endeavour as the success of entrepreneurs more and more hinges on the ability to keep the audience engaged with a content rather than just one-off promotions (Abidin, 2020;Gillespie, 2019).Communicative labour can be defined as the ongoing creation of content, emotional interaction with audiences, responsiveness to the interaction on the platforms, and the performance of entrepreneurial authenticity. These communicative expectations are not gender-neutral and can be seen when comparing the experiences of men and women in the context of feminist media scholarship. Compared to their male counterparts, women entrepreneurs are more likely to be expected to look approachable, to be at the touch of the audience, to be authentic and appear at all times to be emotionally available and good looking (Gajjala, 2018;Gill, 2007;Marlow & Mcadam, 2013). Thus, entrepreneurial communication is both a means of economic production and gendered labour, it produces entrepreneurial visibility and it is not visible as labour.By treating communication as labour, communication scholarship expands to not just focus on the role of communication as a medium for facilitating entrepreneurial learning and leadership, but one where entrepreneurial identities, economic opportunities, and platform visibility are being continually produced.Communicative labour explains how entrepreneurial visibility is produced, whereas emotional branding explains how that visibility is sustained through continuous identity performance and audience engagement.Emotional branding has turned into the vital part of the platform-based entrepreneurship. Unlike traditional companies, social media business owners are increasingly developing a personal identity for themselves, their daily life, emotions and lifestories into entrepreneurial communication to build credibility, trust and maintain relationships with audiences. In the context of creator economies, visibility is not the only way of being entrepreneurial, because the continuous selfdisclosure and relational communication of the creator is also a key entrepreneurial resource (Abidin, 2020;Jane, 2016).However, the communicating expectations at the same time increase emotional pressure on entrepreneurs. Women entrepreneurs have become more and more expected to be 'always on', emotionally attuned, genuine and personally available, whilst at the same time being expected to oversee the performance of the business. These pressures are not due to the fault of individual entrepreneurs; rather, they are a consequence of the nature of the platforms and their algorithms that encourage constant interaction, responsiveness and visibility. Research literature on platform labour is increasingly showing that these are structural conditions of platform labour and control, rather than indicative of individual failures to cope. (Bucher, 2018;Gajjala, 2018;Gillespie, 2019).The developments mirror other cultures of entrepreneurial self-optimisation, where being visible is an ongoing entrepreneurial duty, not just a promotional task.Algorithmic relevance is a key driver of entrepreneurial success and is a process that requires constant content creation, engagement and identity performance. Thus, emotional branding must be seen less as a marketing strategy but as an integral part of communicative labour in which entrepreneurs manage their sustainability on a constant basis in platform economies.The increasing "always-on" entrepreneurialism is noteworthy for the involvement of women, as entrepreneurial work is now part of the performance of identity.Women entrepreneurs are expected to sell products and services, and do it through authenticity, positivity, being emotionally resilient and accessible. Consequently, emotional branding should not be understood solely as a marketing strategy but as an integral component of platform labour. Entrepreneurial success increasingly depends upon the continuous performance of authenticity, emotional accessibility, and relational engagement, reinforcing the interdependence between communication, entrepreneurial identity, and platform capitalism.Women's social media entrepreneurship is often discussed in the narratives of empowerment, independence, flexibility as well as financial inclusion. Digital platforms have clearly increased business opportunities by reducing start-up costs, and providing more flexibility on how to work, and by offering a new avenue for generating income for women who are facing barriers in traditional labour markets (Ghosh et al., 2022;Yu & Sekiguchi, 2024). This progress has enabled numerous women to create innovative businesses, cultivate a sense of entrepreneurship and be more engaged in digital economies.But the opportunities should not be romanticised as an example of unqualified entrepreneurial empowerment. The very same infrastructures of platforms are also those that control visibility, monetisation, audience reach and commercial sustainability by proprietary algorithmic systems as well. Therefore, the structural dependence cannot be completely overcome by entrepreneurial ownership because ongoing communicative work, emotional brand, algorithmic responsiveness and interaction with the audience have become the basis for success in commercial ventures.The theme of empowerment can then be said to have the effect of individualizing entrepreneurial success and to mask the underlying structure that generates entrepreneurial opportunities. Entrepreneurs have limited control over platform governance and algorithmic inequality, non-paid communicative labour, emotional exhaustion, and visibility dependence. As such, the failures of entrepreneurs can then be understood as personal failures that result from larger platforms infrastructures which control economic participation.Moreover, platform entrepreneurship is often not institutionalized in the same way as traditional work with benefits like income security, labour rights, and health insurance, and support measures from the organizations. Women who become entrepreneurs in creator economies in turn then find themselves in a situation of entrepreneurial autonomy and economic precarity, typical symptoms of platform capitalism (Vallas & Schor, 2020;Wood et al., 2019). Gendered forms of online harassment, cyberbullying, reputational attacks and constant visibility anxiety experienced by women as entrepreneurs and creators in platform environments (B. E. Duffy & Meisner, 2023;Jane, 2016) further amplify these structural vulnerabilities.These structural conditions suggest that the experiences of women entrepreneurs cannot be adequately understood through narratives of empowerment alone.Although digital platforms undoubtedly expand entrepreneurial opportunities, they also embed entrepreneurs within communication systems governed by algorithmic visibility, platform policies, and continuous audience engagement. Entrepreneurial success, therefore, increasingly depends upon communicative labour, emotional performance, and sustained platform participation rather than solely upon entrepreneurial capability or innovation. Understanding these intersecting dynamics requires a conceptual framework that recognises both the opportunities created by digital platforms and the structural dependencies they simultaneously produce. This dichotomy of empowerment and exploitation is therefore, not enough to explain women entrepreneurship in the social media. At the same time, the digital platforms open up entrepreneurial opportunities and place entrepreneurs in the network of algorithmic governance, communicative labour, emotional branding and platform dependency. Women's experiences as entrepreneurs are thus not fully empowered nor entirely exploited but rather are ongoing struggles for entrepreneurial freedom and platform dependency. It is necessary to have a conceptual framework that can incorporate both aspects of the dynamics, instead of focusing on just one aspect.Recent scholarship has made significant contributions to our understanding of entrepreneurship in a digital context, including the notions of digital entrepreneurship, platform work, creator labour and platform-dependent entrepreneurship. Digital entrepreneurship is a research field that investigates how digital technologies enable entrepreneurs to develop and generate value for ventures (Nambisan, 2017), creator labour research studies the nature of labour relations, algorithmic governance of platforms (Wood et al., 2019), and visibility labour, content production and audience engagement (Abidin, 2020;B. Duffy & Wissinger, 2017). More recently, platform-dependent entrepreneurship was conceptualised to explain entrepreneurs' increasing reliance on platform infrastructures (Yu & Sekiguchi, 2024). While these views offer valuable insights, they fail to capture the gendered communicative and emotional aspects of platform dependency of women social media entrepreneurs.The present paper does not attempt to say that women constitute a completely distinct category of entrepreneurs. But, it proposes that when entrepreneurial activity is situated in the context of gendered expectations of visibility, authenticity, emotional accessibility and relational engagement, it takes on a different communicative texture and form than platform dependency. The proposed framework is an extension of platform dependency theory, and explicitly includes these gendered communicative processes in the conceptualisation of entrepreneurial dependence. The framework is grounded in the surrounding legacy of research and theory, such as those of creator labour, platform work, influencer research, and emotional labour. These literatures explore various empirical populations but have a shared interest in entrepreneurial activity that relies on the continual communication, audience engagement, algorithmic visibility and emotional performance of platform infrastructures. These literatures, therefore, are used as informative analogues from a theoretical perspective and not as solid empirical data for women entrepreneurs. Empirical future studies are needed on the dynamics of the various types of digital entrepreneurship by women. Communication scholarship needs to shift away from "heroic" projections of digital entrepreneurship and explore the political economy of platform-mediated work critically.First, future studies are needed to examine the impacts of algorithms on the visibility of entrepreneurs and economic inequality. Platform infrastructures have a significant impact on the visibility, engagement and monetisation opportunities that are made available to entrepreneurs.Second, the emotional and psychological implications of the 24/7 digital presence of women entrepreneurs need to be studied. Burnout, anxiety, self-surveillance and emotional exhaustion are becoming more and more central experiences in platform economies.Thirdly, intersectionality needs to be further highlighted in the field of social media entrepreneurship. Platform labour experiences are linked to class, race, geography, language and access to digital technologies, shaping who can participate, gain visibility, and sustain entrepreneurial success within platform-based economies.Communication research, therefore, needs to acknowledge the inequalities in opportunities and vulnerabilities in digital entrepreneurial cultures.Lastly, the study of platform governance and platform labour regulation should be critically addressed by communication scholars. Discourses for entrepreneurship in the present tend to focus on the individual's strength and self-optimisation without holding structural accountability for digital capitalism. Such efforts would contribute to more equitable platform governance and more inclusive digital entrepreneurial ecosystems for women entrepreneurs.Social media entrepreneurship is one of the most salient expressions of today's digital work. Platforms are crucial for women entrepreneurs in terms of economic involvement, creativity and as a space to be more visible as entrepreneurs. These opportunities are, however, parallel to those of precarious job opportunities that are common in the gig economy and platform capitalism.
